Motorcycle Tyres for UK Touring

Your tyres are the only thing connecting you to the road. On a UK motorcycle tour, they'll encounter wet tarmac, gravel, oil patches, white lines, cattle grids, and every surface condition in between. Choosing the right tyres — and maintaining them properly — is the single most important safety decision you'll make before touring.

Tyre Types for Touring

Sport Touring Tyres

The most popular choice for UK road touring. Brands: Michelin Road 6, Bridgestone T32, Continental RoadAttack 4, Metzeler Roadtec 01.

  • Pros: Excellent wet grip (crucial in the UK), long life (6,000-10,000+ miles rear), good feedback, quick warm-up.
  • Cons: Not ideal for any off-road or rough surfaces.
  • Best for: Road-only touring on sportsbikes, nakeds, and sport-touring machines.

Adventure/Trail Tyres

A compromise between road and off-road capability. Brands: Michelin Anakee Adventure, Continental TKC 70, Mitas E-07.

  • Pros: Handle light off-road sections (gravel roads, forest tracks, farm lanes). Good in mud and wet. Robust construction resists punctures.
  • Cons: Shorter road life than pure sport-touring tyres, slightly less precise road feel, can be noisier.
  • Best for: Adventure bikes, mixed-surface touring, Highland single-track with gravel sections.

Touring-Specific Tyres

Designed for maximum mileage and comfort. Brands: Michelin Commander III, Metzeler Cruisetec.

  • Pros: Very long life, stable with heavy loads, comfortable ride.
  • Cons: Less sporty feel, slower warm-up, less suited to aggressive riding.
  • Best for: Cruisers and heavy touring bikes covering big daily mileage.

Tyre Maintenance on Tour

  • Pressure checks: Check pressures every morning before riding, when tyres are cold. Use the manufacturer's recommended pressures for loaded riding (higher than standard).
  • Visual inspection: Look for cuts, bulges, embedded objects, and wear indicators daily.
  • Tread depth: UK legal minimum is 1mm across 75% of the tread width. For touring, replace at 2mm — wet grip deteriorates significantly below this.
  • Carry a tyre gauge: Forecourt gauges are notoriously inaccurate. A compact dial gauge is the most reliable option.
Plan your tyre replacement around your tour dates, not the other way around. If your rear tyre is at 2mm and you're planning a 1,000-mile tour, replace it before you go. Hunting for a specific tyre in rural Scotland mid-tour is no fun at all.

Wet Weather Grip

UK touring is wet touring. Your tyres' wet-weather performance is arguably more important than dry grip:

  • Modern sport-touring tyres (Michelin Road 6, Continental RoadAttack 4) have exceptional wet grip — some of the best ever produced.
  • Full-silica compounds grip well in the wet and warm up quickly — essential for unpredictable UK temperatures.
  • Tread pattern matters: deeper grooves and siping channel water away more effectively.
  • Avoid budget tyres for touring. The £50 saving isn't worth the compromise in wet grip when you're cornering on a rain-soaked Highland A-road.

Puncture Preparedness

  • Carry a tubeless tyre repair kit — plugs, cement, and an insertion tool
  • Carry CO2 cartridges or a mini compressor for reinflation
  • Know where the nearest tyre fitting service is along your route
  • A plug repair gets you to a garage, but the tyre should be professionally inspected and potentially replaced afterward

The right tyres make the difference between confidence and anxiety on wet UK roads. Invest in quality rubber, maintain it properly, and your tour will be safer, more enjoyable, and free of tyre-related worries.
keyTakeaways: Sport touring tyres suit most road-based UK touring, balancing grip, wet performance and mileage.
Adventure/trail tyres add light off-road ability at the cost of on-road grip and life.
Touring-specific tyres maximise mileage and wet-weather confidence for high-mile riders.
Check pressures cold, inspect for damage, and keep tread well above the 1mm legal minimum (2mm+ recommended).
Wet grip matters enormously in Britain, so choose a tyre rated well in the rain.

faq.q: What tyres are best for UK touring?
faq.a: For the vast majority of road-based UK touring, sport touring tyres are the sweet spot. They balance dry and wet grip, offer good mileage, and warm up quickly, which matters on cold British mornings. Choose adventure or trail tyres only if your route includes gravel or unsurfaced tracks, and touring-specific tyres if you cover very high mileages on tarmac.

faq.q: What tyre pressure should I run when loaded?
faq.a: Follow your bike's handbook, which usually lists a higher pressure for loaded or two-up riding than for solo. Check pressures cold, before you ride, because they rise as the tyre warms. Under-inflation causes the tyre to overheat, squirm and wear quickly, and wastes fuel, so carry a gauge and check regularly on a multi-day tour.

faq.q: What tread depth is safe for touring?
faq.a: The UK legal minimum is 1mm across three-quarters of the tread, but for touring you want considerably more. Aim to start a tour with at least 2-3mm remaining, as wet grip drops off sharply as tread wears down. A tyre that is legal but nearly bald is a genuine safety hazard on wet British roads, so replace early rather than risk it.

faq.q: How important is wet grip in Britain?
faq.a: Extremely. Given how often it rains, wet performance should be a top priority when choosing touring tyres. Look for tyres reviewed well for wet grip and confident feedback in the rain, and remember that grip is reduced on cold, damp mornings and over painted lines, drain covers and diesel spills. Ride smoothly and leave extra braking distance when it is wet.
